past_2_weeks.headline: Daily macro and geopolitical brief.
past_2_weeks.summary: Daily macro and geopolitical brief. Figures are the latest available as of the Friday, 2 October close and weekend reporting. Markets are shut for the weekend.

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi’s 23–25 September state visit to Washington produced a managed pause, not a reset. The Busan truce was extended to 10 January 2027, pushing the next hard deadline past the U.S. midterms. The new Board of Trade recommended more favorable tariff treatment on roughly $30 billion of goods in each direction (U.S. agriculture, coal, medical devices and forest products; Chinese consumer goods), with China indicating about 90% of covered items could move toward MFN rates once domestic procedures are finished. Those cuts are not yet in force. Beijing also committed to buy at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal a year in 2027 and 2028. An AI dialogue was formalized. Farm-purchase targets from the May summit remain behind schedule, and Section 301/232 duties, technology controls and rare-earth licensing stay in place.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East
subsections.text: The eight-month conflict remains unresolved after the 17 June memorandum of understanding expired. The U.S. is sending a third carrier strike group plus an amphibious force with roughly 9,000 sailors and Marines; the buildup is expected to be in place by late October or November. President Trump has signaled that renewed strikes are possible after the midterms. A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on 1 October, and an Iranian parliamentary committee advanced a bill that would require transit authorization and fees in the strait. Diplomacy is stalled.

subsections.title: Houthis
subsections.text: Iran-backed forces have used the wider war to press a Red Sea coastal offensive and to strike Saudi targets. The Saudi-led coalition reported a drone hit on a Medina power station feeding the Prophet’s Mosque (one transformer disabled), interceptions of ballistic missiles and drones aimed at Khamis Mushait and Jazan, and airstrikes in Taiz. Washington has so far stayed largely clear of the Yemen fight.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is in a winter-energy phase. Russia has resumed large combined strikes on the grid and is using jet-powered attack drones; three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro were partly closed after repeated hits. President Zelensky said Ukraine is testing five interceptor types and aims for about 400 units by end-October, and that Putin told commanders last month there were “no rules.” Kyiv faces an estimated $27 billion defense-funding gap this year. Russia continues ground pressure and has ordered further army expansion; nuclear rhetoric around Kaliningrad drew a NATO rebuke in late September. No serious ceasefire track is visible.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The operative framework is the extended truce through 10 January 2027. Peak triple-digit tariffs and the sharpest rare-earth and high-tech export controls remain suspended, but the underlying Section 301 and Section 232 regimes are intact. The July 12.5% duties on goods from 60 partners, including China, over forced-labor claims, are a separate track. The $30 billion reciprocal carve-out lists are recommendations only; implementation depends on legal process and a coordinated effective date. U.S. officials are still pressing China on incomplete farm and aircraft commitments. China’s overall trade surplus has stayed very large as exporters reroute through third markets. The short extension keeps leverage on both sides and sets up another cliff in early January.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: USD/JPY is trading in the high 157s to low 158s after touching about 158.44–158.50 this week, a third weekly gain despite the Bank of Japan’s 18 September hike of 25 bp to 1.25% (7–2). The September summary of opinions was read as a slower cadence, and markets roughly halved odds of an October follow-up, with December now the base case. Tokyo core CPI (ex-fresh food) rose 2.7% year on year, above the 2.4% consensus, which briefly supported the yen. Intervention so far is verbal and coordinated in tone. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura have called yen undervaluation a problem; Treasury Secretary Bessent has agreed to closer cooperation on orderly markets. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has also flagged undervaluation. There is no confirmed large-scale yen-buying operation this week. The constraint is fundamental: the Iran-linked oil shock and U.S. yields are widening the rate gap faster than the BoJ is closing it. A disorderly move through 159–160 is the practical line where actual intervention risk rises.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent settled near $102.31 on Thursday (up more than $4) and traded roughly $101.60–$102.60 on Friday; WTI settled near $92.87 and held around $92–$93. Both were set for a modest weekly decline after a large September gain. Drivers pulling in opposite directions: a recovering Saudi export picture versus a third U.S. carrier heading to the Gulf, China’s halt of refined-product exports for October, and a Russian product-export ban running to 31 October. A UKMTO-reported tanker strike in Hormuz added a risk premium. Policy response is shifting from price to physical stocks. The G7 discussed releasing about 100 million barrels of emergency crude and diesel. Washington has pressed Germany and France to draw diesel inventories (reports cite a request on the order of 120 million barrels over six months) or face a possible U.S. diesel-export ban. EIA’s 9 September STEO still assumed Middle East shut-ins averaging about 5.7 million b/d in Q4 and a 2H26 Brent average near $90, with prices easing toward the mid-$70s by 2Q27 if flows normalize. Spot is above that path. Near-term range looks like $98–$107 Brent if the military buildup stays short of renewed strikes and China’s export halt holds; a second tanker incident or resumed U.S. strikes would break the top of that range.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: The energy shock is now the common inflation driver. - United States. The Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh raised the funds rate 25 bp in September to 3.75–4.00%, the first hike since 2023, with the median projection implying at least one more quarter-point move this year. September payrolls rose only 29,000 after downward revisions, missing every Bloomberg estimate. October hike odds fell from roughly 70% earlier in the week to about 20%. The 10-year yield peaked near 5.34% on Thursday (highest since 2002) and traded around 5.21–5.28% on Friday; the 2-year was near 4.81–4.84% and the 30-year near 5.63%. AI-related capex and the fiscal backdrop are keeping term premium elevated even as near-term hike odds ease. - Euro area. Flash September HICP jumped to 3.8% from 3.2%, a three-year high, with energy inflation at 18.8%. Core was 2.5%. The ECB hiked 25 bp on 10 September (deposit rate to 2.50%). Staff see 2026 headline inflation at 3.0%. The 29 October meeting is now live; higher bond yields had been doing some of the tightening, but the inflation print weakens the case for a pause. French budget politics remain a peripheral-spread risk. - Japan. Policy rate 1.25%, next move more likely December than October, as above.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: The cycle is moving from a pure GPU phase into inference, networking, memory, optical connectivity, advanced packaging, power and cooling. Equipment capex outside mainland China is projected to nearly double versus the prior three-year period, but the binding constraints are increasingly upstream. Concentration remains extreme: Nvidia still accounts for the large majority of AI accelerators; TSMC for about 90% of advanced packaging; China for roughly 90% of rare-earth refining used in data-center motors and a dominant share of tungsten used in chip interconnects. Gallium and germanium exports to the U.S. are on a case-by-case license after the November 2025 truce suspended an outright ban, with a continued bar on military end-users. The January truce deadline is therefore also an AI-materials deadline. Power interconnection and transformer lead times, not chip wafers alone, are the practical limit on how fast announced capex becomes operating capacity. The new U.S.–China AI dialogue reduces the chance of a sudden rupture but does not diversify the physical chain.

subsections.text: The same shock runs through every market. A wider Hormuz risk premium lifts oil, which lifts European and U.S. inflation, which keeps the Fed and ECB biased to hike even after a weak payrolls print, which supports the dollar and U.S. yields, which weakens the yen and raises intervention risk, which feeds back into Japanese imported inflation. China’s refined-product export halt tightens diesel just as Washington is asking Europe to release stocks. The U.S.–China truce is the stabilizer for rare earths and AI hardware; its 10 January expiry sits on top of a possible post-midterm Iran decision. Ukraine’s winter grid campaign is a separate energy-security problem for Europe but a smaller oil driver than Hormuz.

past_2_weeks.headline: ## Daily Macro & Geopolitical Report

subsections.title: U.S.–China
subsections.text: President Xi Jinping’s late-September state visit to Washington produced a list of eight “deliverables and understandings” covering trade, a November “super intelligence” dialogue and incident channel, counternarcotics, Iran, and symbolic items (including pandas for Atlanta). The Boards of Trade and Investment first outlined at the May Beijing summit were activated. Military crisis mechanisms, Taiwan, and guaranteed rare-earth volumes were left unfinished. A further Trump–Xi encounter remains possible around APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East
subsections.text: The U.S.–Israel war with Iran, now in its seventh month, is in a tense pause rather than a settlement. President Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal that would halt hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days; Iranian officials later said they had received a U.S. response. Washington is moving additional naval force toward the region, with reporting that three carriers and two amphibious groups could be in place by late November, alongside new sanctions. Iran and its partners have used escalation for leverage: attacks on U.S. warships in the Gulf, strikes on Saudi targets, and Houthi gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including capture of a Red Sea island earlier in September. A Saudi-led coalition has intercepted Houthi drones and missiles aimed at southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh area. Hormuz crude transits have partially recovered (recent estimates near 13 million barrels a day), but the waterway and Bab el-Mandeb remain contestable. Saudi Arabia has pressed for U.S. action against the Houthis; the White House has so far declined a direct fight.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Diplomacy is stalled. Moscow still conditions a ceasefire on territorial concessions Kyiv rejects. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev was in Washington this week on ending the war and possible post-war energy cooperation. On the ground, territorial change in 2026 has been limited relative to prior years (Zelensky has cited roughly 890 square kilometers taken by Russia and about 800 retaken by Ukraine). Russia has opened its winter 2026–27 strike campaign early, with large combined drone and missile packages against Kyiv energy infrastructure, including damage at the Trypillya thermal plant. Ukraine continues deep strikes on Russian refineries and defense industry. Kyiv is scaling interceptor drones against jet-powered loitering munitions and expects additional F-16s from Belgium by year-end.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The Busan truce of October 2025 — which paused triple-digit tariffs and delayed China’s rare-earth export controls in exchange for fentanyl-precursor enforcement and farm purchases — has been extended from a 10 November expiry to 10 January 2027. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed the two-month extension as time to pursue a larger package; Beijing confirmed an extension without initially locking the date. After the Xi visit, both sides published reciprocal lists of non-sensitive goods, about $30 billion each way (2024 import values), for tariff relief. The U.S. list leans toward consumer goods (toys, appliances, tableware, some recreational items). China’s list covers a wide set of U.S. agricultural goods (corn, wheat, meat, dairy, oils; soybeans notably not the centerpiece), medical devices, and other items, with many rates meant to move toward most-favored-nation levels. China also pledged at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal imports in both 2027 and 2028. Farm purchase commitments from the May summit remain behind pace. What did not move: rare earths, advanced technology, and other sensitive lines stay under export controls and case-by-case licensing, including continued restrictions on military end-users for materials such as gallium and germanium. Capital Economics estimates the average U.S. tariff on China only edges from about 22% to roughly 20.5%, still well above pre-2025 levels. Background measures remain: the Supreme Court struck the emergency-tariff regime in February 2026, after which the administration imposed a temporary 10% global duty under another statute, and in July a 12.5% tariff was applied to goods from 60 partners, including China, over forced-labor allegations. The truce is a deadline, not a settlement. ---.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text:
Crude is elevated and two-tiered. As of the 1 October close, benchmark reads clustered around WTI in the low $90s (roughly $91–93) and Brent from the mid-$90s to about $102–103 depending on contract, after the November Brent expiry settled near $103.50 and posted a September gain of about 14%. Prices have been volatile around headlines on Hormuz and diplomacy; the 52-week Brent range runs from the high $50s to about $107. Drivers:
- Partial recovery of Gulf crude flows. JPMorgan has estimated regional crude shipments near 17.5 million barrels a day, about 98% of pre-war levels, while refined-product flows were only about 58%. Hormuz transits have rebounded; Saudi East–West pipeline capacity has been partly restored.
- Product tightness. Attacks linked to the Iran and Ukraine wars have cut refining capacity. China has suspended oil-product exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau, removing flexible diesel and gasoline supply. The U.S. has been urging European allies to draw emergency diesel stocks and is near the end of a coordinated SPR release (up to 40 million barrels cited as the last tranche).
- OPEC+ held October required production at the September level (6 September decision). The next meeting is 4 October.
- U.S. commercial crude stocks were 427.3 million barrels for the week ending 25 September (up 0.9 million). Retail gasoline has been near $4.46 a gallon. Short-term outlook: crude balances can loosen if Hormuz volumes hold and waivers on Iranian loadings continue, which is why some physical benchmarks have softened into contango. Products are the tighter market into winter. Upside risks are a renewed U.S. strike campaign, Houthi disruption at Bab el-Mandeb, or another Hormuz closure. Downside risks are a credible ceasefire and a faster product-export restart from China and the Gulf. ---.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text:
The global bond sell-off is the macro center of gravity. The U.S. 10-year yield touched 5.34% on 1 October, the highest since 2002, before easing to about 5.26–5.27%. The 2-year was last near 4.81%. The third-quarter rise in the 10-year was the largest since 1994. France’s 10-year has approached 5%; Britain’s 30-year has crossed 6%, the highest since 1998. Japan’s yields have moved up with the pack. Inflation is being re-accelerated by energy. Softer U.S. August inflation details did not calm the long end. Euro-area national prints for September beat forecasts: Germany 3.3%, France 3.4%, Italy 4.1%, with the bloc expected near 3.6% versus 3.2% in August. Core in Germany was steady at 2.4%. Policy:
- The Fed hiked last month. Futures still price a meaningful chance of another move at the 28 October meeting (on the order of one-in-three) and further hikes into 2027. Stronger growth, including AI-related capex, is cited alongside oil as a reason not to ease.
- The ECB raised all three key rates by 25 basis points on 10 September, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%. Staff projections put headline inflation at 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028. Markets have priced several further hikes over the next year. The euro-area flash HICP is due today.
- The BoJ is at 1.25%, with the next hike more likely in December than October (see section 3). Higher real yields are tightening financial conditions even without another immediate hike, and they raise the fiscal cost of funding deficits in the U.S., France, the U.K., and Japan. ---.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text:
Hyperscaler capex remains the main private-demand shock. The IEA has noted that spending by the largest technology firms exceeded $400 billion in 2025 and is expected to rise on the order of 75% in 2026, larger than global upstream oil and gas investment. Bain’s data-center work points to multi-trillion-dollar build-out needs by 2030 if announced compute plans are met. U.S. data-center power demand is forecast to rise from about 31 GW in 2025 toward 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW in 2027, with only about 60% of near-term scheduled capacity expected on time. Concentration risks:
- Accelerators: Nvidia still accounts for the large majority of AI accelerator chips.
- Foundry and packaging: TSMC produces about 90% of advanced packaging that integrates logic and memory.
- Lithography: ASML remains the sole EUV supplier.
- Memory: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have shifted capacity to high-bandwidth memory. IDC has projected DRAM revenue up about 177% in 2026; contract prices for conventional DRAM have seen extreme quarter-on-quarter jumps. New capacity is years out, so tightness can run into 2027.
- Materials: China processes roughly 99% of gallium, about 90% of rare-earth metals used in magnets, and a dominant share of tungsten. The truce to 10 January improved the licensing climate versus the autumn 2025 controls, but there are no published volume guarantees, and military end-uses remain restricted. U.S. processing projects cannot replace Chinese supply on this horizon.
- Power and grid equipment: interconnection queues, transformers, and turbines are now binding constraints alongside chips. The Washington “super intelligence” dialogue is a political channel, not a supply commitment. Export controls on leading-edge tools and chips remain the structural fault line under the tariff truce. ---.

Hyperscaler capex remains the main private-demand shock. The IEA has noted that spending by the largest technology firms exceeded $400 billion in 2025 and is expected to rise on the order of 75% in 2026, larger than global upstream oil and gas investment. Bain’s data-center work points to multi-trillion-dollar build-out needs by 2030 if announced compute plans are met. U.S. data-center power demand is forecast to rise from about 31 GW in 2025 toward 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW in 2027, with only about 60% of near-term scheduled capacity expected on time. Concentration risks:
- Accelerators: Nvidia still accounts for the large majority of AI accelerator chips.
- Foundry and packaging: TSMC produces about 90% of advanced packaging that integrates logic and memory.
- Lithography: ASML remains the sole EUV supplier.
- Memory: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have shifted capacity to high-bandwidth memory. IDC has projected DRAM revenue up about 177% in 2026; contract prices for conventional DRAM have seen extreme quarter-on-quarter jumps. New capacity is years out, so tightness can run into 2027.
- Materials: China processes roughly 99% of gallium, about 90% of rare-earth metals used in magnets, and a dominant share of tungsten. The truce to 10 January improved the licensing climate versus the autumn 2025 controls, but there are no published volume guarantees, and military end-uses remain restricted. U.S. processing projects cannot replace Chinese supply on this horizon.
- Power and grid equipment: interconnection queues, transformers, and turbines are now binding constraints alongside chips. The Washington “super intelligence” dialogue is a political channel, not a supply commitment. Export controls on leading-edge tools and chips remain the structural fault line under the tariff truce. ---.

subsections.text: The same three shocks are feeding each other. The Iran war keeps oil and diesel tight, which re-accelerates inflation, which forces the Fed, ECB, and BoJ to stay tight, which pushes global yields to multi-decade highs and keeps the yen under pressure near intervention territory. The U.S.–China truce lowers the odds of a simultaneous rare-earth and tariff shock through early January, which is what allows the AI build-out to proceed, but that build-out is itself a source of power demand, copper and electrical-equipment inflation, and political sensitivity around technology controls. Ukraine’s winter energy campaign adds a second refined-product risk on top of the Gulf. A Hormuz relapse would hit yields, the yen, and AI power costs at once.

past_2_weeks.headline: ## Daily Macro & Geopolitical Report
past_2_weeks.summary: Markets open Q4 against a three-front backdrop: a seven-month U.S.–Iran war that still prices a Hormuz/Red Sea risk premium; a ceremonial but thin Trump–Xi state visit that bought two extra months of trade calm; and a synchronized hawkish turn at the Fed, ECB, and BOJ as energy and AI-related demand keep inflation above target. U.S. midterms in November now sit on top of all three.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: Xi Jinping’s late-September state visit to Washington was the third leader-level meeting since Trump returned to office. Ceremony exceeded substance. The two sides extended the existing trade truce to 10 January 2027, launched a modest “30-for-30” tariff-cut list on non-sensitive goods, opened an AI-safety dialogue, and booked Chinese purchases of U.S. coal. Taiwan, Iran, rare earths, and leading-edge chips were discussed without a public bargain. Xi pressed Washington to “oppose” Taiwan independence; Taipei rejected the framing. Beijing continues to trade with Tehran and has not used its Russia leverage the way Washington wants.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East
subsections.text: The war that began 28 February 2026 is approaching month eight. Diplomacy is live but brittle: a seven-day Iranian trust-building plan is circulating via Qatar, sequencing remains the sticking point, and Trump still says the U.S. will “win very soon” while threatening to “annihilate” the regime if talks fail. Fresh U.S. sanctions hit procurement networks in Russia, China, Hong Kong, and Pakistan. Iran’s rial printed new lows. Houthis have expanded control along Yemen’s west coast and the Bab al-Mandeb, stepped up Red Sea attacks, and struck toward Saudi’s East-West/Yanbu corridor—the main Hormuz workaround. WHO reports 800+ killed in renewed Yemen fighting over two months. U.S. forces were due to leave remaining Iraqi bases this week. China remains Tehran’s economic backstop and, per reporting, a major source of dual-use components seized en route to the Houthis.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is past day 1,680. Russian drone and missile waves on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other cities continued through UNGA week; Zelenskyy called the pattern “terrorism” and said Putin keeps inventing excuses not to talk. Putin says all settlement ideas remain “on the table” but Russia will first weigh its interests after Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory and polling sites. Trump publicly told Zelenskyy to “settle with Putin.” A limited energy-infrastructure ceasefire has not stuck. Washington locked in remaining FY2026 Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funds (~$93 million of a $400 million package) before the 30 September deadline. Putin ordered further army expansion; Zelenskyy warned of more North Korean deployments and $12 billion in planned Russian jet-drone spending. NATO has condemned Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric around Kaliningrad. Winter energy targeting is the next operational risk.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: UNGA highlighted institutional strain: Xi skipped New York for Washington; a search is underway for António Guterres’s successor at year-end. APEC in Shenzhen (18–19 November) is the next leader calendar date; talk of a Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral remains unscheduled.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text:
The Busan-origin truce that capped reciprocal escalation (roughly 30% on many Chinese goods / 10% on many U.S. goods, plus a rare-earths flow arrangement) is now extended from a 10 November expiry to 10 January 2027. That is a two-month bridge, not a reset. After the summit, both sides published “non-sensitive” lists totaling about $60 billion ($30 billion each) recommended for more favorable tariff treatment via a new U.S.–China Board of Trade: - U.S. list (77 Chinese items): toys, holiday décor, fishing gear, tableware, small appliances, car seats.
- China list (~1,619 U.S. items): a wide agricultural basket (soybeans still a notable omission from some cuts), medical devices, coal-related products, personal care. China also committed to import at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and again in 2028. Financial-services access and farm purchase tracking remain under discussion; Beijing is behind earlier farm-purchase run-rates. Average U.S. tariffs on China may ease only modestly (one estimate: ~22% to ~20.5%) and stay well above pre-2025 levels. Sensitive items—advanced chips, dual-use tech, critical minerals outside the truce channel—stay outside the goodwill list. The January 10 clock is the next hard date. ---.

subsections.title: Yen
subsections.text: USD/JPY is around 157 after a July spike toward 164 (40-year lows). Japan and the U.S. Treasury staged a coordinated yen-buying operation in late July (reports in the $50–90+ billion range depending on the window). A separate April–May campaign totaled a record ~¥11.7 trillion. MOF data show no intervention between 27 August and 28 September; verbal defense has done the recent work. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and vice minister Atsushi Mimura have restated that yen undervaluation is “problematic” and that Tokyo is working with Washington. Markets treat 160 as the line that revives live intervention risk.

subsections.title: BOJ
subsections.text: On 18 September the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate 25 bp to 1.25%—a 31-year high—in a 7–2 vote. The hike was not enough, on its own, to re-anchor the yen because the Fed funds range is 3.75–4.00%. Another BOJ move is widely mapped to the 30 October meeting or December if inflation and U.S. pressure persist.

subsections.title: Broader FX
subsections.text: Rate differentials still favor the dollar versus JPY and still-negative or low-rate peers. Intervention is now explicitly a G2 coordination tool, not a solo Japanese circuit-breaker. Carry-trade positioning remains a two-way risk if 160 breaks or if the BOJ accelerates.

subsections.title: Levels (late 30 September prints; highly volatile)
subsections.text: One live Hormuz-crisis tape showed Brent ~$97–98 and WTI ~$90, with a wide seaborne-vs-inland spread. Other sessions in the last 10 days printed Brent from the mid-$90s to above $110 depending on pipeline and transit headlines. The consistent story is a war premium over a recovering-but-not-normal Gulf export base, not a pre-February 2026 $70s market.

subsections.title: Drivers
subsections.text:
- Partial Hormuz disruption plus Houthi pressure on Bab al-Mandeb and Saudi’s East-West/Yanbu system.
- Offset: Middle East seaborne exports recovering toward ~80%+ of pre-war run-rates in September as Saudi pipeline capacity comes back in stages; Iranian loadings have also recovered under waiver talk.
- U.S. SPR releases have met soft demand; Cushing stocks are tight, supporting WTI relative to Brent at times.
- China crude intake earlier in the summer ran well below year-ago levels, capping how far flat price could run even in a deficit tape.

subsections.title: Risks and short-term outlook
subsections.text: Upside: a failed Doha track, a new strike on Yanbu or East-West, tighter Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb, or winter European diesel tightness. Downside: a durable U.S.–Iran pause, faster Hormuz transits, and Chinese demand staying soft. Base case used by several houses is elevated-but-choppy prices through Q4—high $70s to low $90s on a “normalization” path, $90–100+ if the security environment stays the operating regime. Diesel cracks and European gas remain the consumer-price transmission channel.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: U.S. CPI August: +3.4% y/y, +0.4% m/m; core CPI +2.4% y/y, +0.3% m/m. Energy +2.1% m/m; gasoline +3.9% m/m. PCE August (released 30 September): +0.3% m/m, +3.4% y/y; core PCE about +3.0% y/y—softer than some forecasts, still far from 2%. Euro area HICP has been running in the high-2s to low-3s and is expected to jump again on energy in the September flash. Japan’s inflation remains above the BOJ’s 2% target, amplified by the weak yen.

subsections.title: Policy
subsections.text:
- Fed (17 September): +25 bp to 3.75–4.00%, first hike since 2023, unanimous. Median 2026 funds rate lifted to 4.1%. Several officials still flag one more hike this year; October 28 is live but not locked after the softer PCE print.
- ECB (10 September): +25 bp, deposit facility 2.50%. Lagarde called it a “no-brainer.” Next meeting 29 October.
- BOJ (18 September): +25 bp to 1.25%. Next: 30 October.
- RBA: hiked to 4.60%.

subsections.title: Bonds
subsections.text: U.S. 10-year around 5.24–5.26% (29–30 September), up more than 100 bp year-to-date in some tallies; 30-year has traded 5.5–5.6%, multi-decade highs. German 10-year ~3.6%; UK 10-year ~5.4%; JGB 10-year ~3.1%. Mortgage rates above 7% in the U.S. Treasury buybacks in the long end have not capped the sell-off. Energy + AI capex + fiscal supply + a hiking Fed is the common explanation.
Hyperscaler and lab capex is still scaling toward hundreds of billions in 2026 and multi-trillion cumulative buildout estimates through the early 2030s. Constraints are no longer just GPUs.

subsections.title: Concentration
subsections.text:
- Accelerators: Nvidia still dominant in training silicon.
- Foundry / advanced packaging: TSMC remains the bottleneck for leading-edge logic and CoWoS-class packaging; Arizona capacity is years from substituting Taiwan at scale.
- Memory: HBM/DRAM tightness; DRAM revenue forecasts have been revised sharply higher for 2026; Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron have reallocated capacity to HBM.
- Substrates / ABF / PCBs: multi-year shortage talk into 2028–30.
- Critical minerals: China still refines the large majority of rare earths used in motors and cooling; gallium, germanium, tungsten licensing and prior export bans remain a live geopolitical switch. The trade truce only pauses some of that weaponization.
- Power and labor: grid interconnection, transformers, electrical trades, and cooling specialists now delay projects as much as chips. Data-center power demand is colliding with wartime munitions demand for the same industrial base (e.g., Patriot interceptor rebuild vs. rare-earth and packaging capacity).

subsections.title: Financial layer
subsections.text: A growing share of the build is moving from hyperscaler cash into leases, private credit, and structured vehicles. That raises cyclical and refinancing risk if model-revenue ramps disappoint or if rates stay at 5%+ on the long end. Export-control divergence (U.S. chip rules vs. Chinese mineral rules) is the strategic overlay the Trump–Xi AI dialogue has not resolved.

Oil is the hinge. A hotter Iran/Houthi tape lifts gasoline and diesel, holds CPI/PCE above target, keeps the Fed/ECB/BOJ hawkish, supports USD/JPY weakness and yen-intervention risk, and tightens financial conditions into an AI capex boom that already needs cheap power and patient capital. China sits in every channel: rare-earths and packaging for U.S. weapons and AI servers; oil demand that caps crude; diplomatic cover for Iran and Russia; and the January 10 tariff clock. A “stability bargain” (trade truce + coal/farm buys + AI talk) can coexist with proxy conflict. That is the current equilibrium. It breaks if Hormuz/Bab al-Mandeb closes harder, if rare-earth licenses are pulled, or if a Taiwan incident forces the security agenda over the commercial one.

past_2_weeks.headline: Daily snapshot as of early Wednesday Asia time.
past_2_weeks.summary: Daily snapshot as of early Wednesday Asia time. Markets are digesting last week’s Trump–Xi state visit, a still-unresolved seven-month U.S.–Iran war that is spilling into Yemen and the Red Sea, a firming U.S. rates complex, and oil that remains elevated even as some Gulf export volumes recover.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: The three-day Washington state visit (24–25 September) was heavy on ceremony and light on binding outcomes. Both sides framed the relationship as “strategic stability” and “no conflict, no confrontation,” but analysts describe a tactical pause rather than a reset. Concrete items: an AI-incident communication channel with a dedicated dialogue slated for November; work on military crisis communications; operationalization of the U.S.–China Boards of Trade and Investment; and two further leader meetings already booked—APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. Taiwan was raised (Xi pressed for U.S. “prudence”); there was no public resolution on arms sales. Talks also touched Iran and Ukraine. Trump has publicly rejected deeper joint AI-safety work even as the incident channel was announced.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the wider Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.–Israeli campaign against Iran, underway since late February, is in its seventh month. Hormuz remains the core oil-and-gas chokepoint; Iran has used restricted zones, mines, and the threat of further disruption as leverage. Indirect contacts via Qatar and other mediators resumed around UNGA; Washington rejected an Iranian proposal that largely restated earlier terms and did not add meaningful nuclear or strait concessions. Trump has kept three public options on the table—deal, economic strangulation, or much wider force—while denying that the U.S. has offered sanctions relief as a precondition. Yemen is the new second front. After months on the sidelines, the Houthis seized the remaining government-held Red Sea coastline, Mokha, and the Hanish islands in early–mid September, putting Iranian-aligned forces close to the Bab al-Mandab. They have since struck Saudi military and energy sites (including the Riyadh area). The U.S. says it is in direct contact with the Houthis and that the group claims it does not want a fight with Washington; Riyadh has asked for U.S. strikes and has not received them. Saudi- and Yemeni government-aligned forces are now hitting Houthi missile/drone cadres and logistics. The dual-chokepoint risk (Hormuz plus Bab al-Mandab) is the main geopolitical premium in energy.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war of attrition continues. Russia is running large jet-powered drone and missile waves against Kyiv and other cities (the National Academy of Sciences building was hit; data centers and logistics have been targeted). Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps says Operation Vivaldi has retaken about 176 km² north of Lyman across three phases. Moscow is raising 2027 defense spending by a reported 27% and has restricted publication of refinery and energy data after Ukrainian long-range strikes. Drones near the Polish border have prompted Warsaw to revisit air-defense rules of engagement. Neither side is signaling a ceasefire.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: Follow-up Trump–Xi meetings in November–December are now the main scheduled pressure valves in the U.S.–China calendar. Midterm politics in the U.S. (November) constrain how much either leader will give before then.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The year-old tariff truce—U.S. rates on Chinese goods around 30%, Chinese rates on U.S. goods around 10%, plus rare-earth access and agricultural purchase pledges—has been extended two months, to 10 January 2027. That is a short bridge through U.S. midterms and the two remaining 2026 summits, not a durable deal. Under the new Board of Trade “30-for-30” framework, each side recommended about $30 billion of non-sensitive goods for more favorable tariff treatment (~$60 billion two-way). U.S. cuts cover consumer items (toys, fireworks, holiday décor, small appliances, child seats). China’s list covers a wide set of U.S. farm and related products (corn, dairy, meats, some medical devices and materials) but not soybeans. China also agreed to take at least 10 million tonnes of U.S. coal in each of 2027 and 2028. Implementation still requires domestic legal steps; there is no firm start date. What was left off matters more: advanced chips, EVs/batteries, and rare earths. Bessent has said China is meeting the 25 million-ton soybean pledge but lagging other agricultural commitments (~$17 billion). The structure is a managed pause while both sides buy time. ---.

subsections.title: Yen / Japan
subsections.text: USD/JPY is holding around 157.3–157.6, off the late-July spike toward 164 but still historically weak. Officials have reopened the verbal-intervention channel this week: finance chief Satsuki Katayama and currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura have called yen undervaluation a problem and said markets should take U.S.–Japan messages “at face value.” Prime Minister Takaichi made the same point with Trump. The market still treats ~160 as the zone where action risk jumps. 2026 has already seen record yen-buying: roughly ¥11.7 trillion in April–May and ¥15.4 trillion in late July–August, plus the first coordinated U.S.–Japan yen-support operation since 1998 (31 July). Cumulative intervention this year has exceeded prior annual records. Intervention can cap disorderly moves; it has not closed the rate differential that keeps the yen cheap.

subsections.title: Broader CB backdrop
subsections.text: Policy divergence is real but narrower than in 2024–25: the Fed, ECB and BOJ all tightened in September in response to the energy shock. The yen’s problem is still relative carry and Japan’s fiscal/political premium, not a complete absence of BOJ hiking.

subsections.title: Levels (late 29 September trading)
subsections.text: Front-month Brent has been oscillating in a wide ~$103–106 band depending on contract roll and session; WTI has been closer to $91–93. November Brent had been heading for a roughly mid-teens percent monthly gain; WTI’s September gain is smaller but still solid. Intraday moves have been two-sided as export-recovery headlines collide with war risk.

subsections.title: Drivers
subsections.text: - Persistent Hormuz friction and inefficient workarounds (ship-to-ship transfers, night escorts). - Houthi pressure on the Red Sea / Saudi East–West system (Yanbu loadings have restarted after pipeline repairs). - Partial recovery: Kpler data put major Middle East crude exports at ~12.8 million b/d in September, the highest since February, led by Saudi Arabia and the UAE—still below a clean pre-war pattern. - U.S. SPR releases and talk of diesel-tax workarounds on the demand/price-management side. - Diplomacy: hope of a strait-first deal is the main cap cited by traders against a sustained move above $110.

subsections.title: Risks and short-term outlook
subsections.text: Upside: renewed vessel attacks, a closed or tightly rationed Hormuz, Houthi interdiction at Bab al-Mandab, or a breakdown in U.S.–Houthi contacts. Downside: a credible ceasefire-plus-transit package, faster Gulf export normalization, and further SPR barrels. Scenario range in recent bank commentary still stretches from a return toward ~$80 if flows normalize to ~$120 if attacks on shipping intensify. Base case for the next 1–4 weeks: a high, unstable $90s–$110s corridor until diplomacy or a military inflection changes the physical risk.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: U.S. headline inflation remains the energy-and-tariff story. Recent CPI prints have shown monthly headline pops driven by energy (energy up sharply year-on-year) while core has been closer to the mid-2s to high-2s. Official commentary (e.g. New York Fed) still puts overall inflation well above the 2% goal—around the mid-3s on some policy-relevant gauges—and treats tariffs plus Middle East supply shocks as the main 2025–26 impulse. Euro-area HICP was about 3.3% in August, also energy-led, with core nearer 2.4%.

subsections.title: Policy
subsections.text: - Fed: funds target 3.75–4.00% after a 25 bp hike at the mid-September FOMC. Officials are split in public: some (Barr, others) say further adjustment is likely; Williams has stressed that the Committee has time to watch incoming data. Markets have flipped between ~50–70% odds of another 25 bp move on 28 October; December remains live. August PCE is due today (30 September); payrolls follow 2 October. - ECB: deposit rate 2.50% after a 25 bp September hike, framed as insurance against a 2022-style energy second-round. - BOJ: policy rate has been lifted into the ~1.00–1.25% zone (highest in decades); another hike is a live debate for the 30 October meeting, especially if the yen slumps again and imported energy keeps CPI sticky. - BoE: on hold at 3.75%.

subsections.title: Bonds
subsections.text: The U.S. 10-year is around 5.23–5.26%, the highest close cluster since 2007; the 30-year has traded near 5.50–5.62%, multi-decade highs. The move has been more a growth-and-term-premium repricing (strong PMIs, heavy coupon supply) than a one-day inflation scare, but energy keeps the upper tail of inflation live. Japan 10-year yields have also printed multi-decade highs, tightening the global long-end complex. A hot PCE or payrolls print this week would keep October “live”; a soft core PCE would argue for patience and a modest yield fade that still leaves 5% as the new neighborhood, not a ceiling that has been left behind.
The capex cycle is still accelerating even as bottleneck risk is now the dominant analytical theme.

subsections.title: Scale
subsections.text: Consultancies put the 2026–30 data-center build in the $5–6.5 trillion range and ~150 GW of incremental compute. Hyperscaler AI/data-center capex is heading toward $1 trillion-plus by 2028, with financing shifting from internal cash toward more external debt as free cash flow turns. A single 1 GW AI campus is commonly costed at $30–50 billion, most of it IT hardware.

subsections.title: Concentration and chokepoints
subsections.text: - Logic / foundry / packaging: TSMC still dominates leading-edge wafers and a very large share of advanced packaging (CoWoS / SoIC). Arizona and other geographic hedges are multi-year, not a 2026 substitute. - Accelerators: still highly concentrated in a small set of GPU/ASIC vendors. - Memory: HBM/DRAM is the tightest near-term constraint. Forecasts of very large DRAM revenue growth in 2026, contract-price spikes, and supplier comments that the worst shortage may be 2027 are consistent with a multi-year allocation market. ABF substrates and high-end PCBs are a quieter but durable pinch. - Minerals: China still refines on the order of ~90% of rare-earth magnets used in cooling and motors; gallium, germanium and tungsten remain licensing- or ban-sensitive. The trade truce only partially thawed gallium/germanium flows; military end-use remains blocked. - Power and labor: grid interconnection, transformers, and skilled electrical trades are binding in the U.S. and parts of Europe/North Asia. Gulf security risk now also sits on the “where to build” checklist.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: Last week’s Washington state visit (23–25 September) produced pageantry and a “managed stalemate,” not a structural reset. Both sides framed a “constructive relationship of strategic stability,” operationalized the U.S.–China Boards of Trade and Investment, launched an AI dialogue (next session end-November), and agreed follow-up meetings at APEC in Shenzhen (November) and the G20 in Miami (December). Taiwan, advanced-chip export controls, and investment screening were not resolved. Xi pressed for U.S. “prudence” on Taiwan; no joint communiqué closed the gap. Fentanyl precursor controls and two pandas to Atlanta were the low-friction extras.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East (incl. Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.–Iran war remains the dominant energy-security shock. Iran has floated reopening Hormuz within about seven days if Washington eases military pressure and lifts the port blockade; Trump has said a deal is possible after midterms while keeping the “deal or annihilation” framing. Parallel to Hormuz, Houthis have pushed along Yemen’s Red Sea coast toward the Bab al-Mandab, reigniting fighting with the Saudi-backed government (hundreds of combatants reported killed in recent weeks; strikes near Riyadh’s airport). Washington has so far refused Saudi requests for direct strikes on the Houthis, offering intelligence and a division of labor that leaves Riyadh on the Yemen file. Dual-chokepoint risk (Hormuz + Bab al-Mandab) is the live regional threat.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The war is in its fifth year. Russia is leaning on a winter 2026–27 theory of victory built on jet-powered drones and missiles against cities and energy/industrial sites (Kyiv science academy hit; data centers and logistics targeted). Ukraine claims local recapture on the order of ~176 km² in a multi-month push and continues deep strikes on Russian refineries and gas plants. Interception of jet-powered Shaheds is reported around 55%. Diplomatic talk of a U.S.-proposed three-way meeting in the UAE has not produced a date. Poland scrambled aircraft after strikes on western Ukraine. No ceasefire architecture is in place.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: Midterm politics in the U.S. now sit on top of every external file: tariff timing, Iran talks, and China follow-ups are all calibrated to November.

The year-old U.S.–China tariff truce (roughly 30% on many Chinese goods / 10% on many U.S. goods under the prior framework) has been extended to 10 January 2027—a two-month patch, not a durable settlement. Beijing wanted longer; Washington kept optionality through the midterms. On 28 September both sides published the first “30-for-30” lists: about $30 billion each way of “non-sensitive” goods recommended for more favorable tariff treatment (~$60 billion combined). - Into China: large agricultural basket (corn, wheat, meat, dairy, seafood—soybeans not on this incremental list), coal and coal products, timber, medical devices. China also signaled coal offtake for 2027–28. - Into the U.S.: 77 categories—toys, fireworks, Christmas ornaments, household goods, child seats, sporting goods. Over 90% of those lines slated toward MFN-equivalent treatment.

subsections.title: Not covered
subsections.text: advanced semiconductors, EVs, batteries, and the sensitive tech/rare-earth core of the rivalry. Rare-earth access remains governed by the earlier truce (China had pledged restored supply; compliance is still a live test). Section 301 work continues; lists can be revised annually. Two-way goods trade is well below pre-escalation peaks; the U.S. goods deficit with China has narrowed sharply versus 2024. Next hard date: 10 January 2027, with two leader meetings before then.

subsections.title: Yen
subsections.text: USD/JPY is around 157–158 after a bounce from near-160 earlier in September. Officials have re-labeled yen weakness as a problem: PM Takaichi called an undervalued yen “problematic”; Treasury Secretary Bessent discussed “the desirability of a strong yen” with Finance Minister Katayama. Japan and the U.S. already conducted their first coordinated yen-buying intervention since 1998 this summer; Japan’s outlays in the latest campaign ran to a record on the order of ¥15.4 trillion. Markets treat 160 as the intervention tripwire. A further BOJ hike is part of the implicit quid pro quo for U.S. FX support, but fiscal expansion under Takaichi and the still-wide U.S.–Japan rate gap keep the carry trade alive. Intervention risk is a ceiling, not a trend reversal, until the rate gap narrows more.

subsections.title: Broader CB backdrop
subsections.text: Major central banks tightened again in mid-September rather than easing: Fed to 3.75–4.00%, ECB deposit rate to 2.50%, BOJ to 1.25% (31-year high). Divergence is now among hikers (pace and terminal) rather than hike-vs-cut. Dollar strength versus the yen remains the sharpest G10 FX stress.

subsections.text: WTI near $93/bbl; Brent in a high-$90s to ~$98–105 range depending on contract/source after a pullback from mid-September prints above $100–105. Prices remain far above 2025 averages (WTI up on the order of ~45% year-on-year). The Brent–WTI spread has been wide, consistent with seaborne/geopolitical tightness versus U.S. inland supply.

subsections.title: Drivers
subsections.text: (1) Hormuz disruption and tanker/insurance premia from the U.S.–Iran war. (2) New Red Sea / Bab al-Mandab risk as Houthis take coastal ground. (3) Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining, which tighten product markets even when crude headlines ease. (4) Softening from mid-month spikes as markets priced intermittent diplomatic feelers on Hormuz.

subsections.title: Risks
subsections.text: A second chokepoint closing would reprice oil violently. A credible U.S.–Iran arrangement that restores Hormuz flows is the main downside catalyst. OPEC+ spare capacity and U.S. shale responsiveness cap the upside if both straits stay open.

subsections.title: Short-term outlook
subsections.text: Range-bound in the $90s WTI / high-$90s–low-$100s Brent unless either diplomacy or a new Houthi/Hormuz incident breaks the range. Energy remains the swing factor in G7 headline inflation.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: U.S. August CPI: headline about 3.4% y/y, core about 2.4%. Energy has been the headline wild card; core goods/services have cooled more than headline. Euro-area HICP has been running near 3.2–3.3%, again energy-led. Japan’s headline is closer to target, but core-core remains sticky above 3% on some gauges. PCE (U.S. preferred) was still well above 2% on the latest full prints (core PCE mid-3s on a 12-month basis earlier in the summer).

subsections.title: Policy
subsections.text: - Fed: hiked 25 bp on 16 September to 3.75–4.00%. Markets price a sizable chance of another 25 bp in October (~60%+ recently) and further tightening into year-end; the September dots showed a large majority seeing at least one more 2026 hike. Growth data (flash PMI 58.4, 62-month high) and hawkish comments (Barr, Williams) drove the repricing. - ECB: deposit rate 2.50% after the 10 September hike; next meeting 29 October. Meeting-by-meeting, energy-risk biased. - BOJ: 1.25% as of 18 September; next late October. Pace constrained by politics and FX, not by a return to ZIRP.

subsections.title: Bonds
subsections.text: The U.S. 10-year closed last week near 5.18%, highest since 2007; the 30-year touched about 5.50% (post-2004 area). The move has been mostly real yields (growth + supply), not a collapse in inflation expectations. Five- and seven-year auctions tailed. Higher-for-longer is the working assumption until growth or oil breaks.

Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle and peers) are guiding toward the high-hundreds of billions in 2026 capex, majority AI infrastructure; some aggregates put 2026–27 in the $700bn / $900bn neighborhood. The bottleneck has rotated from power (2024–25) toward chips and packaging, with power equipment still a 2027–29 constraint.

subsections.title: Concentration risks
subsections.text: - Logic foundry: TSMC still dominates leading-edge wafers; Arizona ramps help but do not remove the 2026–27 capacity ceiling. - Memory / HBM: SK hynix, Samsung, Micron sold out; 2027 flagged as an extreme tightness year; memory can absorb ~30% of hyperscaler capex. - Packaging / substrates: CoWoS earlier; now ABF substrates and advanced packaging with shortages possibly into 2028–30. - Power & electrical: transformers and switchgear on multi-year lead times. - Minerals: China still refines ~90% of rare earths used in motors/magnets; gallium, germanium, tungsten remain license- or ban-sensitive despite the trade truce’s temporary easing. Helium (fab process gas) and copper/sulfuric acid have been hit by Middle East disruptions. - Trade overlay: AI hardware imports widen the U.S. goods deficit; export controls vs. rare-earth/mineral leverage is the strategic bargain inside the truce. Cost inflation is already visible (Microsoft citing tens of billions of extra component cost). The boom is real; the physical supply stack is the binding constraint, not demand narratives.

Oil and the two straits feed G7 headline inflation, which feeds hike odds, which feed the dollar and USD/JPY, which feed Japanese intervention risk and BOJ politics. The China truce caps one source of goods inflation and rare-earth disruption until 10 January, but leaves the AI stack exposed. Ukraine’s refinery war and Houthi coastal gains are independent oil-supply shocks that can undo a Hormuz diplomatic thaw. AI capex supports U.S. growth and real yields even as it imports geopolitical supply-chain risk from Taiwan, Korea, Japan, and China. Midterms (November) are the political metronome for Trump–Xi, Iran talks, and tariff lists.

subsections.title: U.S.–China / Trump–Xi
subsections.text: Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit to Washington ended Friday 25 September with ceremony and a short list of operational deals, not a strategic reset. The leaders did not resolve Taiwan, export controls, rare earths, or a durable economic framework. They did agree to: an AI-incident communication channel and an AI dialogue in November; a military crisis-communications MOU; an extension of the existing economic truce to 10 January 2027; and recommendations for more favorable tariffs on about $30 billion of “non-sensitive” goods each way. The White House also touted Chinese coal purchases of at least 10 million metric tons in 2027 and 2028 and a U.S.–China Board of Investment; Beijing’s readout omitted those items. Trump said they will meet again at APEC in Shenzhen in November and at the G20 in Miami in December. On Iran, the U.S. said Trump warned that Chinese assistance would be “totally unacceptable” and that Xi “assured him that changes had been made.” Taiwan remained the sharpest unresolved issue: Xi pressed for “prudence”; arms sales and any political understanding were not publicly closed.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran and the Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.-led war with Iran is in its seventh month. Hormuz remains the primary oil chokepoint; a second has opened on the Red Sea. Houthi forces this month seized Mocha and much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, tightening leverage over the Bab al-Mandeb just as Gulf crude’s European route is already constrained. Fighting with Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has intensified (hundreds reported killed in mid-to-late September). Washington has provided intelligence and non-kinetic support to Riyadh but declined Saudi requests for U.S. strikes on the Houthis. Iran has floated reopening Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports; its public conditions otherwise remain maximal. Trump has kept all options on the table, including further strikes, economic strangulation, or a deal after U.S. midterms. Risk of a wider Red Sea disruption and of Iran linking Yemen to any ceasefire remains high.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: The front remains attritional. ISW reports Ukrainian forces shifting toward interdicting Russian reinforcements of small infiltrations rather than immediately clearing every pocket; Ukrainian advances were noted east of Slovyansk and in western Zaporizhia. Russia continues mass drone/missile strikes (Kyiv hit on consecutive nights; Odesa and other oblasts targeted over the weekend). Ukraine continues long-range strikes on Russian oil refining and industrial sites (including the Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar). Zelensky said more than 10,000 Russian troops were killed or wounded in the past week and that Moscow is expanding jet-powered drone production (~$12 billion planned next year). Peace-track noise: reports that Trump asked Zelensky to go to Moscow were denied by U.S. and Ukrainian officials. Putin is leaning on winter energy strikes as a coercive tool; Europe remains the main obstacle in Moscow’s public narrative.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: U.S. midterms (early November) now sit between the Washington summit and the APEC/G20 follow-ups, which will shape how much political capital either side spends on a bigger U.S.–China deal.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The Busan-era truce (tariff pause plus a China commitment to keep critical-mineral flows moving) is extended two months, to 10 January 2027—enough to cover midterms, APEC, and G20, not enough to lock in a multi-year settlement. Bessent framed it as time to work a “bigger deal.” China is behind on some 2026 farm-purchase pledges (non-soy ag) even as soybean volumes have been closer to target. The new, narrower layer is reciprocal tariff relief on ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods each way, via the Board of Trade chartered in May. U.S. exports flagged: agriculture, seafood, logs/wood, cosmetics, medical devices. U.S. imports flagged: small appliances, toys, holiday goods, children’s car seats. Details were slated for further release this week. Rare-earth and high-end chip controls were not dismantled; China had tightened rare-earth export licensing last year in response to U.S. tariffs. The lull lets Beijing keep a large goods surplus and diversify export routes through third countries while talks continue. The January 10 date is the next hard cliff. ---.

subsections.title: Yen / BOJ
subsections.text: USD/JPY spent late September back in the high-150s, with 160 again the intervention watch level after Japan’s Golden Week-style holiday window. The BOJ on 18 September raised the policy rate 25 bp to 1.25% (highest in 31 years) by a 7–2 vote; Governor Ueda said the bank’s focus has shifted from lifting inflation to target toward preventing an overshoot, and he did not rule out consecutive or 50 bp moves. The yen still sold off after the hike because of the two dissents and the unchanged ~250–275 bp gap versus the Fed. Tokyo’s last confirmed-scale operation was late July / early August (estimates ~$53–85 billion of dollar sales, with a reported U.S. rate-check and a small Treasury participation). That bought only a few weeks; the pair retraced most of the move. Authorities remain “ready to act with a sense of urgency.” Rate checks after the September BOJ meeting kept traders on alert. Further yen-buying is more likely on a clean break toward 160 than at 157–158 in thin holiday liquidity.

subsections.text: Advanced-economy policy has re-tightened on energy-driven inflation: Fed +25 bp (16 Sep) to 3.75–4.00%; ECB +25 bp (10 Sep), deposit facility 2.50%; BOJ +25 bp to 1.25%. Downside: a credible U.S.–Iran pause that restores Hormuz volumes, or a Saudi-led de-escalation in Yemen. Base case for the next 1–2 weeks: high-volatility range, Brent biased $95–110, with geopolitical headlines dominating inventories. Energy remains the main imported inflation shock for the Fed, ECB, and BOJ.

PCE remains the Fed’s preferred gauge and has run hotter than core CPI on a 12-month basis earlier in the year. - Euro area HICP: 3.3% in August (from 2.9% in July); energy inflation jumped. ECB staff: headline 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027, 2.1% in 2028. - Japan: underlying CPI approaching 2%; BOJ now flags overshoot risk from wages and imported energy.

Officials cite inflation still above 2% and a resilient economy/AI capex. - ECB: deposit rate 2.50% after 10 September hike; not pre-committed to a path; energy scenarios show a wide inflation range. - BOJ: 1.25%; next hike more likely 1Q27 unless yen/energy force an earlier move.

The rise is mostly real yields, not a blowout in inflation breakevens. Higher term premia plus war-risk and heavy issuance keep the long end sensitive. A second Fed hike would keep 10s bid above 5% until growth or oil clearly cools.

Hyperscaler and AI-campus capex for 2026 is in the high-hundreds of billions (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft on the order of ~$650 billion combined in some tallies; Stargate and other campus projects add more). Tehran’s public conditions remain maximalist. Houthis used the war to seize Mokha port and Perim Island, tightening leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb after Hormuz disruption shifted Saudi exports toward Red Sea ports. They have struck Riyadh, Yanbu, and other Saudi sites; Washington has so far limited itself to intelligence sharing rather than direct strikes on the Houthis, while Trump has kept military options against Iran on the table. G7 ministers called on Iran to end support for the Houthis.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Fighting continues with no ceasefire. Overnight Russian strikes killed civilians in Zaporizhzhia and Sumy; Ukrainian long-range drones hit Russian industrial sites and oil infrastructure (including a halt at the Perm refinery after a fire). Russia struck logistics near Odesa. Zelenskyy said Moscow shows no readiness to end the war and is investing in jet-powered drones; Lavrov blamed Europe for blocking talks. Trump has urged Zelenskyy to “settle with Putin.” The conflict is now past day 1,676.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: Korean Peninsula issues were discussed at the Trump–Xi talks but produced no public breakthrough.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text:
The Busan (Oct 2025) truce that rolled back triple-digit tariffs and paused rare-earth and high-tech export restrictions is extended only to 10 January 2027—a short “compliance period,” not a durable settlement. New, limited substance:
- Reciprocal “more favorable tariff treatment” on about $30bn of non-sensitive goods each way (U.S. farm goods, seafood, wood, cosmetics, medical devices into China; Chinese small appliances, toys, holiday goods, car seats into the U.S.), via a new U.S.–China Board of Trade. Final rates and product lists are expected Monday from USTR Greer.
- China is meeting the 25mnt soybean purchase track but lagging the $17bn other-ag commitment; rare-earth deliveries have also been described as lagging.
- Average bilateral tariff rates remain high (on the order of mid-30s percent U.S. on China and ~31% China on U.S., after layered IEEPA/Section 301/122 actions and exemptions). The January deadline, APEC, and G20 are the next pressure points. Export controls on advanced chips and China’s rare-earth licensing remain the strategic core of the dispute. ---.

subsections.title: Yen / BOJ
subsections.text: USD/JPY closed Friday near 157.3 after a 1%+ rebound in the yen (as strong as ~156.94). Officials flagged an “undervalued” yen: PM Takaichi called weakness “problematic”; Bessent discussed “the desirability of a strong yen” with Finance Minister Katayama. Markets treat ¥160 as the intervention tripwire. Japan spent a record ¥15.4tn (~$96–99bn) buying yen between 30 Jul and 26 Aug, including a rare coordinated U.S.–Japan yen-buying operation (first since the 2011 earthquake intervention; the 1998 analog is often cited for yen-buying). BOJ raised the policy rate to 1.25% on 18 Sep (highest in 31 years) but two dissents and limited hawkish guidance left the yen vulnerable until verbal intervention and hike bets reasserted. Rate-check rumors preceded Friday’s bounce.

subsections.title: Broader CB trend
subsections.text: The Fed, ECB, and BOJ are all in a modest tightening or “higher-for-longer / hike-if-needed” stance because energy and residual goods inflation have not fully faded. Coordinated FX action is back as a live tool when disorderly moves threaten imported inflation (Japan) or global bond-market spillovers.

subsections.title: Levels (Fri 25 Sep settlement)
subsections.text: Brent $104.32 (−2.1%); WTI $92.41 (−2.3%). Brent is roughly flat to slightly up on the week; WTI is down ~8% on the week. The Brent–WTI spread is the widest since May (~$12), reflecting U.S. diesel-export-ban talk (which would strand product in the U.S. and cut refinery runs) versus still-tight seaborne crude and product markets.

subsections.title: Drivers
subsections.text:
- Geopolitical premium: Hormuz disruption earlier in the war; Houthi pressure on Bab el-Mandeb and Saudi facilities; Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining.
- Offset: hopes of a U.S.–Iran phased reopening of Hormuz; Kpler tracking showed ~33.7mnt of crude still leaving Hormuz in the week of 20 Sep.
- EIA: U.S. crude stocks +3.0mnt to 426.4mnt (week of 18 Sep); gasoline and distillates drew.

subsections.title: Outlook
subsections.text: Range-bound but two-tailed: a credible Hormuz reopening could pull Brent toward or below $100; a Houthi closure of Bab el-Mandeb or renewed U.S.–Iran kinetic action would push it higher. Diesel and heating-oil tightness remains the inflation channel into winter.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: Latest detailed U.S. CPI: August headline +0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y; core +0.3% m/m, 2.4% y/y. Energy remains the swing factor in headline; core is cooler than mid-year peaks but still above the 2% target on PCE. Fed SEP (Sep): 2026 PCE 3.7%, core PCE 3.4%. ECB staff: euro-area headline 3.0% in 2026, still above target into 2028. Energy and AI-related goods/power demand are the two persistent shocks.

subsections.title: Policy
subsections.text:
- Fed: hiked 25bp on 16 Sep to 3.75–4.00% (unanimous; first hike since 2023). Median dots imply another 25bp by end-2026 (year-end midpoint ~4.1%). Next FOMC: 28 Oct. EFFR ~3.88%.
- ECB: hiked 25bp on 10 Sep; deposit facility 2.50%, MRO 2.65%, MLF 2.90%. Staff see more energy-driven inflation; markets price another hike by December. Next meeting 28–29 Oct.
- BOJ: policy rate 1.25%.

subsections.title: Bonds
subsections.text: U.S. 10-year yield ~5.17% (25 Sep), highest area since 2007 after a mid-week spike to ~5.20% on strong flash PMIs and auction indigestion. 2-year has traded near 4.9%. Higher real rates plus war-risk premia are tightening financial conditions even as AI capex supports growth.

Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle and peers) are guiding toward several hundred billion dollars of 2026 capex, majority AI infrastructure; multi-year data-center build estimates run into the low trillions. The binding constraint has shifted from power (2024–25) back toward chips and memory, with power, transformers, and interconnects still long-lead.

subsections.title: Concentration risks
subsections.text:
- Logic / packaging: TSMC ~90% of advanced packaging; Nvidia still dominant in training accelerators.
- HBM / DRAM: SK hynix, Samsung, Micron sold out; SK hynix has called 2027 the tightest supply year on record.
- Tools: ASML EUV booked through 2027–28.
- Minerals: China ~90% of rare-earth refining, high shares of gallium, germanium, tungsten; 2025 export controls were only partially eased under the truce. Helium and electronic-grade chemicals remain fragile after Middle East disruptions.
- Power & grid: 1 GW AI campus often cited at $30–50bn, majority IT hardware; transformer and interconnect lead times stretch into 2027–28. U.S.–China AI safety talks do not liberalize chip or rare-earth trade. A January truce lapse or new licensing crackdown would hit this stack first.

Oil-war risk feeds headline inflation, which keeps the Fed/ECB hiking and the 10-year elevated; high U.S. yields and a firm dollar keep USD/JPY near intervention range, forcing Tokyo (and occasionally Washington) into the FX market. The same energy shock raises AI build costs (power, copper, helium, shipping). The U.S.–China truce is a two-month option, not a reset: rare earths and advanced packaging sit at the intersection of the trade war and the AI boom. Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb plus any Hormuz relapse is the fastest path back to $110+ Brent. Ukraine’s refinery campaign adds a second, smaller supply shock to middle distillates.

subsections.title: U.S.–China Relations (Trump-Xi Summit, Sept 23–25)
subsections.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping completed a three-day state visit to Washington. The meetings featured extensive ceremony (airport greeting, state dinner, National Archives visit, panda diplomacy) but limited concrete policy breakthroughs. Main outcome: A two-month extension of the existing trade truce (originally from the 2025 Busan understanding) until January 10, 2027. Both sides signaled willingness to continue talks on a broader deal covering tariffs on roughly $30 billion of non-critical goods, agricultural purchases, and financial services. China is meeting soybean volume targets but lagging on other agricultural commitments and consistent rare-earth deliveries. No major progress was reported on Taiwan (Xi pressed for stronger U.S. opposition to independence; no public change in U.S. policy), AI governance, the Iran conflict, or Ukraine. Leaders agreed to meet again at APEC (Shenzhen, November) and the G20 (Miami, December). Analysts described the summit as “pomp over substance,” with both sides buying time while core strategic differences remain.

subsections.title: U.S.–Iran Conflict & Middle East
subsections.text: The war of attrition continues after the collapse of the June 2026 Memorandum of Understanding. Iran has floated new proposals (including a seven-day path to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under certain conditions), but gaps remain large. The U.S. continues economic pressure and targeted strikes; Iran maintains resistance on nuclear and navigation issues. Iran-backed Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on targets in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities near Yanbu (Red Sea export hub). Saudi forces intercepted many of the projectiles. These actions keep pressure on energy infrastructure and shipping.

subsections.title: Ukraine–Russia
subsections.text: Fighting continues without major frontline breakthroughs. Russia has conducted large drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other cities. Ukraine continues long-range strikes on Russian energy and refinery targets. At the UN, Zelenskyy pushed for tighter sanctions and floated limited energy-related ceasefire ideas ahead of winter; Russia shows little interest in meaningful talks short of maximalist demands. The U.S. has invited Putin to the G20 in Miami.

subsections.title: Other
subsections.text: Netanyahu faced a walkout of dozens of delegates during his UN General Assembly speech. Broader UN week highlighted ongoing gridlock on multiple conflicts.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The dominant near-term development is the short U.S.–China trade truce extension to January 10, 2027. This suspends certain tariffs and maintains rare-earth flows while talks continue. Expectations for a comprehensive deal remain low; both sides are managing a fragile “hostile but interdependent” relationship. Broader U.S. tariff actions earlier in 2026 included new 10–12.5% duties on goods from roughly 60 partners (framed around forced-labor enforcement). Tensions persist with Canada and others. EU–China frictions and discussions of closer Canada–EU ties have also drawn U.S. tariff threats. Supply-chain reconfiguration and “friend-shoring” continue as structural responses.

subsections.title: Japanese Yen
subsections.text: Intervention risk remains elevated. The yen has weakened toward the 159–160 area versus the dollar after the Bank of Japan’s recent rate hike (to a 31-year high near 1.25%) failed to deliver sustained strength. Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has reaffirmed that the principles of the July 2026 coordinated U.S.–Japan intervention (the first major joint yen support in decades) remain in place. Japan spent a record amount (over ¥27 trillion year-to-date in some tallies) on interventions in 2026. Rate checks have been reported, and markets are watching closely for further action if volatility intensifies.

subsections.title: Broader Trend
subsections.text: Central banks continue gradual diversification away from the dollar (more plan to reduce USD holdings than increase them over the next decade). Interest in gold, the euro, and the renminbi has risen amid geopolitical risk. FX interventions overall have increased year-on-year. Other emerging-market central banks (e.g., India) have intervened to support local currencies amid global rate and oil pressures.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Oil remains the dominant near-term swing factor linking geopolitics to inflation, growth, and policy. Brent and WTI have been volatile. After jumping on Houthi attacks and limited U.S.–Iran progress (Brent briefly near $106–107), prices eased somewhat into the low-to-mid $90s / around $105 range depending on the contract and exact timing (as of late Sept 25 data). Global inventories have drawn down significantly. Upside risks include further Houthi/Saudi infrastructure damage, renewed Iranian actions, or prolonged Hormuz/Red Sea constraints. Downside risks center on diplomatic progress or faster Middle East production recovery. The EIA projects Brent averaging around $90 in the second half of 2026 before declining toward the mid-$70s in 2027 as production recovers. Extreme disruption scenarios from some banks still flag potential spikes well above $100 (or higher). Higher oil feeds directly into inflation, central-bank decisions, growth drag (especially in energy-importing Europe and Asia), and risk sentiment.

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.text: U.S. headline CPI held around 3.4% year-over-year in recent readings, with energy contributing meaningfully. Core measures have eased somewhat (near 2.4% in some prints) but remain sticky in services. Persistent oil above $90–100 keeps headline inflation elevated and complicates the path back to the Fed’s 2% target.

subsections.title: Monetary Policy
subsections.text: The Federal Reserve has been in a hiking cycle (policy rate recently in the 3.75–4.00% range or higher). Markets have priced further increases if inflation stays elevated. The ECB and others have also tightened. AI-driven investment is providing growth support that partially offsets energy-related drag.

subsections.title: Bond Markets
subsections.text: The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to multi-year highs (recently ~5.2%), with the 30-year reaching levels not seen since 2004. Drivers include sticky inflation, resilient growth (partly AI-supported), heavy Treasury issuance amid large fiscal deficits, and a higher term premium. Higher yields raise borrowing costs, support the dollar (complicating some currency interventions), and interact with trade and geopolitical risk premiums. Many forecasts see the 10-year remaining in a 4.5–5.0%+ range near term (“higher for longer”).

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Massive AI-related capital expenditure (data centers, chips, power infrastructure) is a major growth engine, especially in the U.S., helping keep overall growth resilient despite energy and trade shocks. However, the supply chain is highly concentrated and geopolitically fragile: - Advanced packaging: TSMC controls ~90% of capacity. - High-bandwidth memory (HBM): Dominated by three suppliers (SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron); demand is expected to exceed supply well into 2027–2030. - Critical minerals: China refines ~90% of rare earths used in magnets, motors, and cooling systems. China has already used export controls on gallium, germanium, and other materials as leverage (some suspended under the current trade truce until early 2027). - Other bottlenecks: Lithography (ASML), specialty gases/chemicals, transformers and power equipment (long lead times into 2027–2029), and data-center energy demand straining grids. Any escalation in U.S.–China tech controls, rare-earth restrictions, or Taiwan-related tensions could constrain AI hardware availability, raise costs, and slow the capex boom supporting growth and equities. Diversification efforts are underway but will take years.

subsections.text: These factors form a tightly linked system: Geopolitics (Iran, Houthis, U.S.–China) → Oil prices → Inflation → Central-bank policy & yields → Currencies & intervention risk → Feedback into trade and growth. AI investment acts as a partial offset to energy and trade drags but introduces its own concentration risks. Fiscal deficits and bond supply keep upward pressure on long-term yields.

past_1_month.outlook: The environment remains one of elevated volatility and fragmented risk. Growth is supported by AI and resilient U.S. demand but faces headwinds from energy costs, sticky inflation, and geopolitical uncertainty. Policy responses (monetary, fiscal, and trade) will continue to be data- and event-dependent, with the January 2027 U.S.–China deadline and ongoing Middle East developments as key near-term markers.
